#6059. Brazil’s Economic Impasse

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

MONICA DE BOLLE is Senior Fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics, an Adjunct Professor at Georgetown University, and a co-author of The New Economic Nationalism.

Neither Lula nor Bolsonaro Can Solve the Country’s Problems

On October 5, the day after the first round of Brazil’s general elections, the country’s financial markets were euphoric. Brazil is struggling with high debt and low growth, and investors are eager for leaders to reduce budget deficits, deregulate, cut taxes, and perhaps even privatize state assets. After nearly four years under the left-wing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known as Lula, who has been slow to implement such measures, investors hope a right-wing government will create opportunities for bold reform.

Rule by the right might be exactly what Brazil gets. The far-right Liberal Party made substantial gains in the legislature, becoming the single largest party in both the Senate and the Chamber of Deputies. Its presidential candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of the notorious former President Jair Bolsonaro, led the aging incumbent, Lula, by nearly two percentage points in the first round of voting. Lula has shown himself capable of impressive political comebacks, but Flávio Bolsonaro is still the favorite in the runoff vote scheduled for October 25.

Even if Bolsonaro wins, however, the prospects for the Brazilian economy are dim. The policies he has put forward are nothing close to the substantial fiscal consolidation program that will be necessary to bring down debt and stimulate private investment, and his determination to weaken Brazil’s political institutions creates the kind of uncertainty that scares investors away. Economic growth has been sluggish under Lula, whose administration has struggled to relieve the high debt burdens afflicting the public sector and households. What would truly doom the country to economic crisis, however, is the kind of authoritarian-inspired politics that a Bolsonaro government could usher in.

Brazil is in serious economic trouble. The country’s sovereign debt ratio has ballooned to 83 percent of GDP, fiscal deficits leave no room for additional government spending, and high interest rates are hurting consumers and investors. Meanwhile, the Iran war has raised the price of fuel and other goods, weighing on household balance sheets already strained by high debt and leaving many Brazilians desperate for leaders who can alleviate their daily hardships.

This predicament is years in the making. Before Jair Bolsonaro was elected in 2018, his predecessor, President Michel Temer, enacted a cap on public spending to contain Brazil’s runaway fiscal problems. Temer introduced the cap as a constitutional amendment to prevent future governments from changing the spending ceiling to suit their needs. Yet Jair Bolsonaro raised the cap several times anyway, which required convincing Congress to amend the constitution. In return, the executive branch effectively ceded control of the budgetary process to the legislature.

Lula therefore inherited a system in which he had little room for fiscal adjustment, and he made few attempts to fix the problem during his term. The result was high budget deficits and persistent inflation, which forced the central bank to raise interest rates substantially. In turn, high interest rates damaged household balance sheets and lowered overall investment and growth.

If Lula were reelected, he would find it incredibly difficult to introduce new fiscal reforms and other measures to support growth. He promised to reduce spending and has proposed a comprehensive overhaul of Brazil’s tax system, which would help increase the budget surplus and reduce public debt. Yet Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party and its allies now hold a majority of seats in the Senate and the Chamber of Deputies, allowing them to block any legislation Lula might pursue.

Yet it is overly optimistic, if not completely unrealistic, to expect that Bolsonaro would fare better. Neither candidate has provided much detail during the campaign about what he would do to fix the economy. Bolsonaro has instead spoken often about “institutional reforms,” which he has said would include amending Brazil’s 38-year-old constitution to make existing labor and environmental regulations more flexible, among other changes; meddling with the Supreme Court; and granting amnesty to his father, who is serving a prison sentence for leading a 2023 coup attempt. Those steps are likely to drive away investors because stable institutions are necessary for an economy to function well. A government that undermines the judicial system and the constitution will compromise the integrity of its economic policies, no matter what those policies are or how good the reputations of the officials making them may be.

Gathering support for such an overhaul of the country’s political institutions, moreover, would require compromises that could worsen Brazil’s economic troubles. To secure enough votes in Congress to advance Bolsonaro’s priorities—for example, two-thirds of the Senate would need to approve the removal of a Supreme Court justice, and three-fifths of both houses must approve a constitutional amendment—the government would have to bring legislators outside its coalition on board. Those politicians would almost certainly demand substantial funds for their constituencies in exchange for their support, adding to the budget deficit.

Bolsonaro’s far-right movement will also be focused on holding together its recently formed coalition of governors, mayors, and voters. Much of its constituency is lower-middle-class Brazilians who rose out of poverty during the boom years two decades ago, while Lula was serving his first two terms in office. After seeing their income growth stagnate in the years since, these voters have turned to the Liberal Party, but their loyalty is new. Most are self-employed and face economic precarity. Both Bolsonaro and Lula are now trying to appeal to these voters by promising initiatives that boost income and offer household debt relief, but delivering such programs—if it is even possible—would only exacerbate Brazil’s economic woes.

What Bolsonaro has shared about his economic policies does not inspire much confidence, either. His party has said it would reduce government spending by $40 billion, or 1.5 percent of GDP, and deliver primary budget surpluses—a measure of the budget balance that does not include interest payments. But it has not explained how it would accomplish this, nor has Bolsonaro elaborated on his vague plans for controlling the rise in public debt. Ultimately, it is unlikely that Bolsonaro can deliver on any of these promises, especially if he keeps his pledge not to cut pensions and key social programs.

Part of the problem is that the Liberal Party’s economic program lacks a viable plan for reducing costs. It proposes eliminating at least ten government ministries but has no estimate of the resulting cost savings. When Jair Bolsonaro took similar steps after he assumed office in 2019, removing cabinet positions and laying off public servants, those moves had little effect on fiscal outcomes. Other promised measures include reducing Brazil’s value-added tax, phasing out a tax on financial transactions, lowering taxes on electricity and fuel, spending $180 billion on infrastructure over four years, and building 2.5 million new homes. None of them would fix Brazil’s fiscal problems; they would only make those problems worse.

The same goes for the rest of Flávio Bolsonaro’s tax plan. His economic advisers have said they intend to reverse every tax created or raised under Lula’s finance minister, Fernando Haddad. Haddad’s tax increases were intended to shift the tax burden to high-income brackets, raise government revenue, and reduce inequalities in the tax system. These taxes have contributed to a modest increase in revenue but fell short of delivering budgetary surpluses. Bolsonaro has argued that the measures are impeding investment because they tax higher income brackets more heavily, but there is no evidence to support this idea. Instead, repealing all these tax increases would worsen Brazil’s fiscal situation. A simple calculation shows that Brazil needs to increase its primary budget balance by about six percent of GDP, either through increased revenue or decreased spending (or both), to keep its debt from rising further. That adjustment would have to be spread over at least three years, giving indebted households and firms time to change their consumption and investment patterns, to avoid a recession. Slashing taxes, however, would reduce government revenues, raising the debt.

Brazil’s high interest rates are another constraint. The central bank’s current rate is 13.75 percent, astronomical by Latin American standards, dictating interest rates everywhere in the economy. Public debt service payments alone consume some 8.7 percent of GDP. Bolsonaro would not be able to lower interest rates significantly without sparking a recession, so he would face the same problem that has plagued Lula during his latest term—few good options for containing a rapidly growing debt.

Neither Lula nor Bolsonaro is well positioned to solve Brazil’s economic problems. A decisive turn toward illiberalism under Bolsonaro, however, would all but assure economic disaster.

Flávio Bolsonaro has never disavowed his father’s championing of Brazil’s dictatorship, which lasted from 1964 to 1985, and his Liberal Party traces its lineage to the party that sustained the military regime. Moreover, he has pledged to release his father and his father’s associates who are in prison for staging an insurrection and a coup attempt in 2023. Flávio’s brother Eduardo Bolsonaro, a former member of Brazil’s Congress who would likely play a significant role in his brother’s government, has openly expressed his admiration for Viktor Orban’s illiberal regime in Hungary, claiming a desire to learn the “best practices” of a movement that rewrote Hungary’s constitution, reshaped its courts, silenced its press, and deployed other overtly authoritarian tactics. And the substantial far-right bloc in Brazil’s Congress supports policies to undermine institutions, including by impeaching members of the Supreme Court—a step these parties advocated even before corruption allegations emerged against several of the court’s justices. (Flávio Bolsonaro is also under investigation for his involvement in the same corruption scandal.)

Although Brazil is not at risk of returning to military rule, the former authoritarian regime serves as a warning of what could happen if a Bolsonaro administration follows its illiberal inclinations to their logical conclusion. During those two decades of military dictatorship, Brazil spent at unsustainable levels, mostly funding state enterprises, to preserve the regime’s hold on power. The country defaulted on its public debt, endured corrosive hyperinflation, and saw income inequality skyrocket. Six economic stabilization plans failed and growth stagnated. Brazil is not alone in this experience. No Latin American country that swung from democracy to authoritarian rule in the past century has benefited economically from the shift. Countries elsewhere in the world that prospered after such a transition, including some in East Asia, became less authoritarian during their economic ascent.

Brazil’s rightward shift fits a regional pattern. The common thread that unites Brazil with Argentina, Chile, and Colombia is the crude libertarian worldview that each of their far-right movements espouse. All of them talk about citizens becoming entrepreneurs free of the state. They tell voters who have unstable employment and little economic security that their policies will bring prosperity. But their populism rarely wins the confidence of investors. Like its peers, when the Brazilian far right says it can overcome the country’s substantial problems with institutional demolition and a threadbare economic agenda, what it really offers is empty promises.

#6057. House Dem who defied Hakeem Jeffries scores upset win in pro-Trump district

'The Big Money Show' panel analyzes President Donald Trump's economic messaging on the campaign trail and reviews the latest Fox News polls in the Ohio and Texas Senate races ahead of the midterm elections, where cost of living remains a top concern for voters.

A Democratic lawmaker who publicly defied House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., twice beat the odds to win re-election in a district that President Donald Trump carried in 2024.

Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, D-Wash., defeated Republican Washington State Sen. John Braun to win a third term in the House of Representatives, The Associated Press reported.

It's an important victory for House Democrats in their quest to claw back the majority in Congress, but one that could also create drama for party leaders on key votes over the next two years.

JEFFRIES THREATENS 'SERIOUS RESPONSE' AFTER DEMOCRATS HELP GOP ADVANCE ANTI-SOCIALISM VOTE

Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, D-Wash., arrives for a vote series at the U.S. Capitol on Sept. 25, 2024, in Washington, D.C. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Gluesenkamp Perez, who has been known to buck her party on votes in the past, infuriated her fellow Democrats twice in September when she sided with Republicans on procedural votes that helped GOP leaders rescue their agenda from conservative rebellions.

If not for her and Rep. Jared Golden, D-Maine, siding with Republicans on those two votes, the House GOP's agenda would have been paralyzed.

The first time earned her a rare public rebuke from Jeffries, who called it a "breach of trust." Other left-wing lawmakers called for her to be removed from the powerful House Appropriations Committee over the move.

But one could argue that Gluesenkamp Perez's public defiance of her own party was critical for her political survival. Trump won her district by roughly 3 percentage points in 2024, and she first won her seat by defeating an incumbent House Republican.

President Donald Trump looks on during the trophy ceremony after the U.S. Team wins 17-13 following the Sunday's Singles on day four of the Presidents Cup 2026 at Medinah Country Club on Sept. 27, 2026, in Medinah, Ill. (Luke Hales/Getty Images)

Washington's 3rd Congressional District includes rural areas and the city of Vancouver, and smaller coastal towns in the southwest portion of the state.

HOUSE DEMS OVERWHELMINGLY REJECT ANTI-SOCIALISM RESOLUTION AFTER 2 MODERATES DEFY JEFFRIES

Part of what bolstered Gluesenkamp Perez in her previous two races was her opponent, Joe Kent, suffering from electability issues because of his association with far-right groups. He was later named Trump's director of the United States National Counterterrorism Center, but resigned over disagreements on Middle East policy.

This time, however, the race was expected to be much closer, with Braun running as a more mainstream GOP candidate.

Joseph Kent, director of the National Counterterrorism Center, during a House Homeland Security Committee hearing in Washington, D.C., on Dec. 11, 2025 (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Braun is a former Navy captain who also helps run his family's company, Braun Northwest, a manufacturer of emergency vehicles.

More than $20 million was spent on their race, according to The Washington Standard, a sign of its critical position for both parties.

#6056. Chinese AI Stocks Are Slumping, Too

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

China Brief: Chinese AI Stocks Are Slumping, Too

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

The highlights this week: China grapples with a slowly deflating artificial intelligence bubble, officials in Beijing keep their eyes on the U.S. midterms, and China and Pakistan launch an “information corridor” amid anxiety around their Belt and Road Initiative projects.

The highlights this week: China grapples with a slowly deflating artificial intelligence bubble, officials in Beijing keep their eyes on the U.S. midterms, and China and Pakistan launch an “information corridor” amid anxiety around their Belt and Road Initiative projects.

U.S technology stocks are suffering a downturn amid worries about artificial intelligence overvaluation, but China’s AI market bubble has been slowly deflating for months.

The country’s STAR 50 index of science and technology companies is down by more than 40 percent since July, leaving it nearly 200 points below where it was at the start of the year. The overall Shanghai stock exchange has also drifted down this year, but tech companies saw a significant rise until the summer, followed by a larger decline.

It’s hard to pinpoint a clear reason for this drop. My own feeling is that the highest-quality U.S. AI models widened the distance with their Chinese counterparts this year, but that isn’t widely reflected in standard AI performance indexes, where the gap has largely stayed constant, falling somewhere between six to eight months for Chinese models to catch up with their U.S. equivalents.

The increasingly strenuous compute demands of high-end AI are hard on Chinese firms, which possess a fraction of the computing power of their U.S. counterparts. That caused some cutbacks in providing services through the AI agents that are uber-popular in the country, but that was already the case when Chinese AI stocks were still rising in the first part of the year.

My sense is that the stock decline isn’t specific to AI, but reflects a wider downturn in market confidence among the small Chinese investors who make up the majority of the market. That fits with the general doldrums of China’s post-COVID economy; Beijing is struggling to get the wind back in its sails, but the public isn’t willing to play along.

As usual, state-backed investment firms are injecting capital back into the markets under official instructions; this is still unlikely to staunch the bleeding. But the correction isn’t as painful for Chinese AI firms as for their U.S. equivalents.

The stock market is much less central to the Chinese economy, accounting for just 5 percent-6 percent of household investments. And Chinese AI firms have less private investment than their U.S. counterparts; the real backing likely comes from opaque government funding, especially since DeepSeek’s ferocious takeoff in early 2025.

Still, while U.S. President Donald Trump’s White House froths about so-called superintelligence, the Chinese government is more skeptical—especially about AI’s impact on labor. Recent official comments confirm that Beijing wants more balanced investment. AI firms may find it hard to get traction with the Chinese leadership if they’re not delivering for the whole economy.

Conveniently, one of the best tests of Chinese economic sentiment is upon us. Nov. 11, or “Double 11” day, usually sees large e-commerce discounts and a bonanza of spending. It once concentrated on the day itself but now spreads across a few weeks. Battered consumer confidence may produce worse sales numbers than normal.

Online spending on goods is up by 4.3 percent so far this year—respectable, but a far cry from the double-digit growth of the pre-COVID years. A weaker spending season points to another quest for any way to get the economic engine revving again in 2027.

Beijing’s U.S. midterms reaction. With a Democratic Party comeback likely in the U.S. midterms on Tuesday, China could welcome a weakened Trump—set to be more concerned with maintaining his slipping grip on power than in starting new trouble abroad. Trump has been meek toward China since it turned off the flow of critical minerals, scoring a victory in their trade war.

Meanwhile, Chinese state media coverage of the U.S. elections has hit the usual notes used to try to discredit foreign democracies, emphasizing that financial influence and corrupt interests supposedly dominate voting.

China has benefited from the fracturing of U.S. politics in a number of ways. Chief among them is that counterintelligence work has fallen apart thanks to the politicizing of U.S. agencies and the reluctance to share information. But there is some caution that Democrats might return focus to human rights issues ignored by Trump—and subsequent investigations into China.

China-Pakistan corridor doubts. There is some anxiety around the future of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), the most vaunted part of the Belt and Road Initiative. Last week, the two countries launched a “China-Pakistan Information Corridor” to rebuke criticism—but there is clearly doubt on the Chinese side.

Only about half the promised funding for CPEC has ever materialized, and Beijing refused to cough up for a major railway upgrade, leaving the U.S.-backed Asian Development Bank to step in. Attacks by Baloch separatist militants along the corridor have intensified in recent months; China has offered to provide further security, but Pakistan seems cautious.

Threats to Chinese nationals in Pakistan have risen, making firms reluctant to send personnel. Chinese scholars have told me that kidnappings for ransom in the country have gone unreported after the Chinese companies involved paid up.

Moon landing plans. China’s ambitious space plans now officially include a crewed moon landing before 2030. That has been in the cards for a while and will be an occasion of genuine patriotic joy when it happens. Chinese science fiction has imagined a place among the stars for the nation for more than a century.

I don’t think a moon landing will reignite a space race with the United States, though. After all, nearly 60 years have passed since the United States made it to the moon; crewed rockets are mostly a PR stunt given how much more robotic probes can do for actual science.

The real Sputnik moment will come when China manages something that the United States hasn’t achieved, such as the not-so-distant prospect of a manned Mars mission in the 2030s.

Nvidia’s Chinese links. U.S. intelligence last year exposed a woman with a “close relationship” with Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia and a Trump tech ally, as an alleged Chinese asset—to no avail. The White House refused to act on the news or to create any firewalls to limit Huang’s considerable access within the administration.

China hawks inside the U.S defense world have expressed concern about Huang’s influence for some time, largely because Nvidia’s interests and U.S. interests do not correlate. Huang advocates selling advanced chips to China and was able to persuade Trump to allow some such exports in return for the White House getting a 25 percent cut.

Nvidia may be trying to reduce the impact of the spy plot story by imposing new restrictions on its data center partners, which can now only let Chinese firms make up a minority of their sales.

#6055. DeSantis calls GOP midterm losses 'extinction-level event' — and explains why Florida survived

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis sounded off Wednesday on Republicans' massive nationwide losses, while analysts consider whether his vocal responses are positioning him for a nationwide run.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis warned Wednesday that Republicans have been nearly wiped out nationally after devastating election losses, while highlighting his state as the lone remaining GOP stronghold among the 10 most populous states as speculation builds about his political future in 2028.

Tuesday was an otherwise brutal night for the GOP, as the Trump movement faces major questions amid setbacks in longtime Republican strongholds such as Kansas and Texas, while holding Senate seats in West Virginia and deep-red Wyoming and South Dakota.

"This is close to an extinction-level event for Republicans… out of the 10 largest states in this union, only one state will have Republican control of their state, the state of Florida," DeSantis said at a Wednesday news conference.

DEMOCRATS SEIZE MAJORITY OF GOVERNORS’ OFFICES IN ELECTION-NIGHT SHIFT

DEMS SEIZE THE SENATE AS BLUE TIDAL WAVE CRASHES DEEP INTO TRUMP COUNTRY, TOPPLES GOP STRONGHOLDS

"We've built up a record of achievement. We've earned trust from a number of our voters that, even in the worst situation that you can imagine politically, we were able to hold the line," DeSantis added.

Fox News Digital reached out to DeSantis for comment.

Orlando-based political strategist and pollster Doug Kaplan told Fox News Digital that DeSantis appears to be eyeing a lasting role on the national stage.

"I think last night was a big night for DeSantis. If you're looking at winners on the Republican side, then I think he's found his lane if he wants to run for president in 2028," he said.

Kaplan characterized DeSantis' comments as an "opening salvo" in an effort to distance himself from the Trump-led status quo in the Republican Party, though he acknowledged the staying power of Trump's MAGA movement among GOP primary voters.

DeSantis also highlighted his own push for the election-cycle buzzword "affordability" in Florida.

Amendment 3 passed with about 62% of the vote Tuesday. It increases homestead property tax exemptions from $50,000 to $250,000 by 2028.

"The existence of Amendment 3 on the ballot is one of the reasons Florida averted the fate of other red states. It drew more voters to the polls," DeSantis said, highlighting an issue on which Republicans still won decisively.

Kaplan predicted Vice President JD Vance and Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, may also follow DeSantis’ tack. Both men saw their party take major losses in their home states, he noted, citing Vance’s former Senate seat going to Democrat Sherrod Brown.

DeSantis highlighted losses in Cruz’s home state but did not reference the senator: "Texas has been the most significant Republican state this century. A Democrat sweep of statewide races — and possible capture of the legislature — takes away one of the anchors of the modern GOP. A huge loss," DeSantis said, echoing his point that Florida remains the only one of the 10 most populous states with a Republican governor.

AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI

Gov. Ron DeSantis speaks during a press conference at Florida International University on Aug. 26, 2026, in Miami. (Al Diaz/Miami Herald/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)

He pointed to stunning upsets that included Kansas, Texas, Georgia, North Carolina, South Carolina and potentially Mississippi — which hasn't elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since segregationist Sen. John Stennis' last term in the 1980s.

"If Mississippi goes down, that will give Dems 56 Senate seats," DeSantis said. The Magnolia State emerged as perhaps the biggest surprise of the morning, with Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith trailing Scott Colom, a Democratic state district judge from Lowndes County, by about one-tenth of 1% in a race most Republicans didn’t even have on their radar.

Former Miami Mayor Francis Suarez, a Republican whose now-Democrat-run city maintained a 3-1 Republican advantage in its congressional delegation, credited DeSantis with helping set the stage:

"We had a great outcome, right? And I think the 1.5 million-vote registration advantage that Gov. DeSantis took four years to build was actually the firewall that prevented Florida from going down the same path as Texas or Michigan," Suarez told FOX Business’ "Big Money in the Morning" on Wednesday.

"Republicans need to simplify their message. They need to be message discipline like Democrats were in this cycle. And then they got to find young, articulate, attractive candidates like the Democrats have found."

Speaking with "Straight Shooter" host Stephen A. Smith on Election Night, DeSantis similarly argued that voters supported conservative policies on some ballot measures while rejecting Republican candidates, suggesting a disconnect between the party's agenda and its appeal to voters.

Former senior Senate advisor and political strategist Mary Marslender told Fox News Digital that DeSantis is doing what any successful governor would in this scenario.

"He’s taking a victory lap on a winning record. That doesn’t means he’s distancing himself from Trump or the MAGA movement. DeSantis successfully focused on state-level results: tax relief, public safety and electoral success, all while underscoring Florida’s position as a reliable conservative stronghold," Marslender said.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis speaks with President Donald Trump as he arrives at Southwest Florida International Airport in Fort Myers, Fla., on Oct. 23, 2026. (Reuters)

"If congressional members in Washington could have done the same, we would have seen a very different outcome these midterms. We should expect to hear more from DeSantis on Florida’s proven results and his approach to governance in the run up to 2028."

"I think the timing of Governor DeSantis's comments is pretty clear. Republicans have to confront some very difficult election results and now make a decision on how to make forward," said Elizabeth Pipko, a former RNC national spokesperson.

"He shares a lot of great ideas with President Trump... It will be interesting to see if they choose to work together in some way and how that leads into 2028."

For DeSantis, who will leave office in January after his unsuccessful 2024 presidential bid, the question is whether Florida's success will remain a state-level victory lap or become the foundation for a renewed national political role ahead of 2028.

#6054. What Israel’s Election Won’t Change

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

ALUF BENN is Editor in Chief of Haaretz and a Senior Fellow at the Bill Graham Centre for Contemporary International History at the University of Toronto.

The Constraints and Costs of the New Security Consensus

When Israelis go to the polls on October 27, much of the world will be rooting for the defeat of the country’s longtime prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. Under his nearly two decades of rule, Israel has become steadily more aggressive. It has abandoned any pretense of supporting a two-state solution; started constructing hundreds of new Jewish settlements in the West Bank; and, following Hamas’s cross-border attack on October 7, 2023, laid waste to the Gaza Strip, occupied parts of Lebanon and Syria, and launched war against Iran, its archnemesis. Meanwhile, its democratic institutions have faced endless attacks by Netanyahu and his allies, who have proposed laws that would, among other things, greatly curtail the power of Israel’s courts. Should he return to power for an unprecedented seventh term, many fret that the country will permanently transition into a rogue theocratic actor.

To many voters, this election thus marks a crucial turning point in Israeli domestic policy. The prime minister’s main political opponent, former Israel Defense Forces Chief Gadi Eisenkot, holds a more liberal worldview than his competitor. He supports an independent judiciary, a free press, and a professional civil service. Should he win, he will likely try to reverse Netanyahu’s efforts to curtail each institution’s independence.

But an Eisenkot victory is unlikely to change Israel’s foreign policy or approach to the Palestinians. Almost all of Israel’s Jewish political parties, Eisenkot’s included, are opposed to Palestinian statehood, not just Netanyahu’s Likud. They all believe that Israel’s brutal war on Gaza was morally just and practically necessary. And almost all of them think that Israel was right to attack Iran and to establish and create what its government and military call “security zones”—occupied territory—in Lebanon and Syria. In fact, the only real disagreement between Eisenkot and Netanyahu on matters of security is whether the latter made the right tactical decisions in each of these conflicts, such as when Netanyahu rejected a cease-fire in Gaza that would have freed Israeli hostages earlier.

That is not to say he will follow exactly the same course. Eisenkot and Netanyahu differ in important ways on the barrage of West Bank settler attacks against helpless Palestinians, which are aimed at driving them out of their land. The prime minister, committed to his far-right allies, shrugs off the issue, whereas his competitor calls their behavior “Jewish terror.” Even if Eisenkot has little pity for the Palestinian victims, he realizes that the West Bank is on the verge of a bloody explosion and that Israel is at risk of even greater international opprobrium because of its reckless policy there. But overall, no matter what happens in the elections, Israel will continue to repress the Palestinians and strike its enemies. It will thus face diplomatic and economic costs, as the country’s frustrated partners begin cutting off aid and perhaps even enacting sanctions.

There are many issues at play in Israel’s election. Politicians, for example, have debated ultra-Orthodox exemptions from the draft, Netanyahu’s corruption charges, and what, if anything, the government should do about Jewish terrorism. But on the whole, the contest has been focused on who is to blame for failing to stop Hamas’s October 7 attack, which killed 1,200 Israelis and resulted in 251 more being taken hostage in one day. The opposition has argued that Netanyahu is responsible for the country’s worst-ever security failure, pointing out that he sustained Hamas with Qatari money, ignored intelligence warnings about Hamas plots, and then blocked an independent investigation into what happened. Eisenkot, who lost a son and two nephews to fighting in Gaza, has been particularly unsparing in his criticism, repeatedly hammering Netanyahu for refusing to take any accountability for the calamity. The prime minister and his supporters, for their part, have brushed off these accusations. Instead, they have blamed October 7 on the military and security services. They have also promoted conspiracy theories that there is what Netanyahu’s cronies and supporters call “treason from within”—or that someone inside Israel helped facilitate Hamas’s brief invasion.

But despite this blame game, both sides agree on the tragedy’s primary lessons: that Israel is surrounded by diehard merciless enemies and that the Palestinians can never be trusted. This attitude is, in part, a raw expression of anti-Arab racism, which is more visible in Israel’s post–October 7 Jewish society. But it is also an electoral play. If the polling is correct, Eisenkot will need the support, however tacit, of Israel’s two Arab parties to put together a government. Netanyahu is thus trying to win over voters who, much as they hate him personally, cannot stand the idea of a government propped up by Palestinians.

This strategy is unlikely to work on liberal Israelis, who view this election as the last chance to save their homeland from sliding into dictatorship. Many Israelis who live abroad, including immigrants who left the country because of Netanyahu’s leadership, thus intend to come home and vote for his replacement. But these election day visitors and likeminded liberal voters are rallying to protect and preserve their way of life in a country that is becoming more religious and nationalistic. And even many of the anti-Netanyahu voters would be unhappy about partnering with the Arab parties to replace the current government. Few would bother to think about the two-state solution, viewing the idea as a relic from the overly optimistic 1990s. Eisenkot, the current leader of this electorate, has declared his personal opposition to a Palestinian state, as have Israel’s other centrist and conservative opposition figures. Only Yair Golan, the leader of Israel’s sole left-wing Jewish party, supports what he calls “separation from the Palestinians” and a return to diplomacy—and even he lacks a plan for how to make that happen.

In one sense, the country’s rejection of a two-state solution is not new. The last detailed negotiations over Palestinian statehood took place in early 2001. Most Jewish Israelis turned against the idea following the second intifada and Hamas’s 2007 takeover of Gaza. Netanyahu has railed against Palestinian sovereignty for his entire political career. (His brief ostensible endorsement of such a state, in 2009, was heavily conditioned and widely considered insincere.) And after October 7, opposition to the notion has become far more resolute. Before the attack, some major Jewish parties would still pay lip service to the notion of making peace with the Palestinians, and their politicians expressed tentative openness to a settlement. Now, they either reject it out of hand or simply dismiss the issue altogether.

Israeli officials have also become far more aggressive. The country may have turned against Palestinian independence years ago, but for most of the last two decades, it avoided full-scale wars and preserved the low-cost status quo. That restraint, even if disrupted by periodic rounds of fighting with Hamas, endeared Netanyahu to mainstream Israelis, who could pretend that the conflict was a thing of the past and all but forget about the Palestinians. Yet this attitude changed when Hamas crossed the border. Afterward, Israel adopted its current policy of destruction and occupation—which Netanyahu’s election campaign is bragging about, since it knows that bombing Iran and invading Gaza, Lebanon, and Syria have been extremely popular among the population at large. The prime minister’s main opponents all endorsed these tactics—criticizing him only for failing to achieve his pledge of “total victory.”

Netanyahu, in turn, blamed Eisenkot for being soft on Hamas when he served in the country’s war cabinet. Eisenkot then said that he had voted for a more aggressive invasion than what the prime minister ultimately undertook. Eisenkot later pledged to “end Hamas rule in Gaza within 18 months” if elected. This line is not necessarily as hawkish as Netanyahu’s posture, since it suggests a willingness to consider diplomatic means of removing the group from power. Eisenkot has also strongly criticized Netanyahu’s campaign pledge to overthrow the Iranian regime. Instead, he supports measures to take the enriched uranium out of Iran and to put its nuclear program under a verification regime. “You can’t overthrow a government from the air; it’s a delusion,” he said. But he nonetheless backed bombing the country to weaken its military and nuclear program, even if he disagreed with the ultimate end.

The rest of the world, of course, does not share Israel’s view. Quite the contrary—in the wake of the destruction of Gaza, polls show that Israel’s international approval ratings have hit new lows. Politicians in every region are arguing that Israel is guilty of major human rights violations, with many claiming that the country has committed genocide. Even some of Israel’s friends are warning that the state has gone overboard. In July 2025, for example, U.S. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer declared that although Israel “has a right to defend itself and end Hamas’s brutal rule,” the “reporting and images out of Gaza—depicting the devastating levels of hunger, starvation, suffering and death—are wholly unacceptable.”

Outside countries are also particularly furious about its settlement expansion in the West Bank, which cannot be justified as a reaction to October 7. As a result, sanctions have reached Israel’s shores. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband declared on September 8 that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank is unlawful and announced a sanctions regime against the settlements and companies involved in their financing and construction. Given that London is a major financial center, Israeli banks—which are financing the major settlement projects—are now in trouble.

Across the Atlantic, Israel still has the support of U.S. President Donald Trump, who has endorsed Netanyahu’s reelection campaign. But most of the Democratic Party’s politicians—and even many Republicans—now want to stop or limit U.S. aid and technology transfers to the Israel Defense Forces, citing the use of American munitions in the destruction of Gaza. Many prominent Democratic Party officials want to sanction the country, too. If Democrats take control of at least one house of Congress in the midterms, the United States could stop sending blank checks to Israel.

Israelis generally attribute such rising international anger to anti-Semitism instead of sincerely held concerns about the rights of Palestinians, Middle Eastern stability, or the proper allocation of military resources. But they are nonetheless aware of their growing isolation and fear that, after the election, they might get hit by what former Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak has called a “diplomatic tsunami.” This assessment is widely accepted in the mainstream media and by Netanyahu, who argues that only he—with his superior English skills—can stop such an onslaught, much as he maneuvered to stop the Biden administration from ever imposing real consequences on the country for its war in Gaza. The Israeli right wing has been arguing for many years, with justification, that Israel can continue its occupation and denial of civil rights to the Palestinians while manipulating the international community with hasbara (public diplomacy and lobbying). Eisenkot, by contrast, will try to win the world back by being upfront about what his country is willing to accept and then negotiating honestly—two things that Netanyahu has rarely done.

Eisenkot’s approach would likely win over more international partners, at least for a time, as did the leaders of two other former military chiefs, Barak and Yitzhak Rabin, who unseated Likud governments. Netanyahu has burned so many bridges with his parade of lies that Eisenkot would probably get an international grace period simply by virtue of his relative honesty. And Eisenkot might indeed make changes that please Israel’s partners, such as slowing settlement construction. He opposes the controversial E1 settlement project, which is aimed at slicing a future Palestinian state by half, and has pledged to tackle Jewish terrorism.

But eventually, Eisenkot would disappoint any overseas Israel supporters who expect a thorough reversal of Netanyahu’s foreign and Palestinian policies. And even if he somehow changed his own mind on Palestinian statehood—which he insists he has never supported—his freedom of action would be severely restricted by his governing coalition. Eisenkot’s power bloc relies on two right-wing parties whose leaders strongly oppose the two-state solution and mistrust the Palestinians. One of them, Avigdor Lieberman, even wants to dismantle the Palestinian Authority and bring in Jordan to rule over the Palestinians who reside in the West Bank (an idea that Amman rejected decades ago). They would bring Eisenkot’s government down if he expressed openness to a Palestinian state.

Polling shows that the October 27 election will be extremely tight. In fact, if the surveys are right, neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu will win an outright majority. The country is thus likely to experience a period of horse-trading, as both politicians jockey to peel off the other’s partners. Netanyahu might even try to lure Eisenkot himself into a kind of unity government, promising to put his judicial overhaul or other culture-war campaigns on hold in return. (Eisenkot has adamantly rejected the idea of serving under Netanyahu, even for a rotation, but about-faces have been a staple of Israeli coalition politics.) Alternatively, negotiations could fail, and the country would almost immediately return to the polls. It would not be the first time that an Israeli contest failed to produce a lasting government: the country held five general elections from 2019 to 2022 before its political leaders established a coalition that could hold on to power for more than 12 months.

But no matter the outcome—a Netanyahu caretaker government, a Netanyahu majority government, a unity government, a minority Eisenkot cabinet supported by the Arab parties, or even an Eisenkot majority government—Israel’s next prime minister will keep occupying parts of its neighbors and brutalizing the Palestinians. He will thus have to contend with Israel’s increasing isolation from the rest of the world. The government might end up spending even more on local arms production to replace U.S.-funded systems, working hard to bypass export controls on military and dual-use items (as sanctioned Iran and Russia do today, and as Israel did in its early years). Israel might face its ultimate fear—losing the United States’ veto at the UN Security Council, which has protected its occupation since 1967 from international censure, even under critical Democratic presidents such as Jimmy Carter and Barack Obama.

This may not be the outcome that Israelis actually want. But without a sea change in how they think about their problems, it is the one they are careening toward. The odds, however, are particularly pronounced if Netanyahu and his partners stay in power. In that case, more liberal Israelis will not wait to see how badly the world punishes their country. They will instead flee to pursue their way of life in a quieter place.

World Brief: Iran Strikes and Israel Aid Cuts Shake Up Election Day

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at U.S. strikes on Iran, future U.S.-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine, and a challenge to Australia’s landmark social media legislation.

As Americans head to the polls in today’s midterm elections, two last-minute foreign-policy developments could impact voters’ decisions.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at U.S. strikes on Iran, future U.S.-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine, and a challenge to Australia’s landmark social media legislation.

As Americans head to the polls in today’s midterm elections, two last-minute foreign-policy developments could impact voters’ decisions.

On Monday—election eve—the United States attacked Iran’s Qeshm Island, targeting an anti-aircraft facility in what U.S. officials described as a defensive measure amid reports that Iran was planning missile strikes. “It’s just a minor attack. It wasn’t war,” U.S. President Donald Trump told Fox News Tuesday morning.

Prior to the strikes, Iran’s foreign ministry said Monday that it would reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the United States agreed to a set of demands, and Trump posted on Truth Social that a settlement “could happen!” Monday’s attack makes such a deal seem unlikely in the near term, however. On Tuesday, senior Iranian security official Mohsen Rezaei wrote on X that “America’s response to Iran’s rights and demands was not convincing.” Rezaei, who is the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, is the official to whom U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance recently sent a letter in an attempt to find common ground on negotiations.

Many analysts fear that Trump may be planning to renew large-scale offensive strikes on Iran following the midterm elections. According to reports in recent weeks, Washington has relocated troops in preparation for an escalation, deployed a Patriot missile defense system to Israel, and urged several Gulf Arab countries to prepare for a military campaign.

The war and its economic repercussions have been a focal point in the midterms, with a September-October Pew survey reporting that around two-thirds of Americans disapprove of Trump’s handling of the conflict. Mark Zandi, the chief economist of Moody’s Analytics, estimated that the Iran war has cost the average American household an extra $2,000. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has resulted in soaring gas and diesel prices—up 43 percent and 68 percent, respectively, since the war started—and price increases in global commodities from condoms to Diet Coke.

American voters cite the economy as the top issue in this year’s elections, and if polls forecasting a Democratic takeover of both the House of Representatives and the Senate prove correct, Trump’s war in Iran could be partly to blame. However, if Democrats do win in the Senate, they will have the power to decide whether to stop funding the war, Sen. Chris Murphy told Foreign Policy in October.

U.S. support for Israel has also been a key issue in the midterms, with many progressive Democrats making ending that support a central campaign talking point. And on Tuesday, in what some are interpreting as a last-ditch effort to prevent a blue wave, Trump abruptly announced that the United States would cut off $4 billion in aid to Israel by the end of the year.

Washington currently provides Israel with $3.8 billion annually in military assistance, part of a 10-year deal lasting through 2028 that was struck under former U.S. President Barack Obama. Ending that agreement early would likely require congressional support.

“The left uses the $4 billion payment—that everybody knows about, it’s no secret—as a signal of unfairness, and we can’t allow that to happen,” Trump said.

He said that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had agreed to the deal “months ago.” In May, Netanyahu voiced a desire for the U.S.-Israel relationship to move “from aid to partnership.”

However, Israel’s defense ministry seemed blindsided by the news. “We were surprised by the president’s statements, especially today,” a spokesperson told Israeli media. “We are in ongoing talks with the Americans. We will study the implications.”

Another push for peace. Russia confirmed Tuesday that it will participate in a new round of U.S.-mediated negotiations with Ukraine to end the war. According to special envoy Steve Witkoff, the working-level talks will take place in Abu Dhabi from Nov. 10 to 11 and will “focus on post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace.” U.S. first lady ‌Melania Trump will convene Russian and Ukrainian representatives at the White House on Thursday in a separate attempt to foster goodwill between the parties.

The diplomatic efforts come after Russia bombed a humanitarian aid hub in the Ukrainian village of Komyshuvakha on Monday, killing 31 and leaving dozens missing. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has indicated that Ukraine will participate in the Abu Dhabi talks, but he said the latest strikes cast doubt on Russia’s willingness to pursue peace.

“There was a moment when the next steps could have shown that progress toward peace was possible,” Zelensky said in a post on X on Monday. “With these killings, Russia is sending an entirely opposite signal: Russia is counting on more killings.”

Access denied. South Africa and Rwanda will be suspended from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), effective Jan. 1, 2027, for not meeting eligibility criteria, the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative announced on Monday. The agreement, enacted in 2000, allows sub-Saharan countries to export goods to U.S. markets without paying duties.

Eligibility to participate in AGOA is reviewed annually. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement Monday that the two countries are being removed for engaging in practices that “pose a threat to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests in the region.” The statement also cited concerns about rule of law and human rights in Rwanda, corruption in South Africa, and barriers to U.S. trade and investment in both countries.

The news is stoking anxiety in South Africa, where unions are urging lawmakers to push back against the move, citing risks of thousands of job losses across automobile, manufacturing, and agricultural sectors. The South African government, which said it was prepared for the possibility of suspension, said it recognized these concerns and will continue to pursue diversification of its exports. The Rwandan government has yet to officially respond to the news from Washington.

Ban blowback. On Tuesday, Australia’s highest court began hearing challenges to legislation that bans social media use for youth under age 16. A Sydney-based digital rights advocacy group and the social media platform Reddit are pushing back against the landmark law that they say restricts freedom of expression for Australia’s young people.

The groups argue that the ban, enacted in December 2025, infringes on the rights of youth to participate in political discussion, pointing out that social media is where youth get their news and can engage in debate as they approach voting age. Reddit is one of 10 social media sites—along with TikTok, Instagram, and X, among others—that would be required to restrict the age of its users under the law.

Australia is among more than 60 countries worldwide pushing for legislation restricting social media usage for children—but Australia’s model may be the “most severe,” FP’s Alexandra Sharp reports. The laws aim to protect youth from harmful content and limit the impact of social media on developing brains, such as algorithmic content models designed to keep people on their phones.

The Collins English Dictionary has selected its word of the year: “mogging.” Defined as “the act of outshining or outperforming someone or something,” the term is most popular in Generation Z and Generation Alpha circles and is often used in the context of physical appearance. According to copywriter Rachel Quin, the word likely originated from the term “AMOG,” or “alpha male of the group,” which became popular in bodybuilding circles in 2016.

Maxine Davey is an editorial fellow at Foreign Policy.

Maya Krainc is an editorial fellow at Foreign Policy.

#6052. Thune to run for minority leader

Senate Republicans are preparing to make the transition from the majority to the minority — and their top leaders will seek to retain their positions in the 120th Congress, even after the political drubbing they endured Tuesday night.

Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., will run for minority leader during next week’s GOP leadership elections, a spokesperson for his office said.

After enjoying a 53-47 majority, he will face a very different chamber next year, with Democrats looking to control between 54 to 56 seats, depending on how the dust settles.

In a post on X just after midnight on election night, as the extent of the losses became clear, Thune wrote, “Over the last two years, Senate Republicans have put up a strong record of accomplishment that’s created safer streets, more money in Americans’ pockets, and new opportunities for families and businesses to get ahead.”

“As we head into 2027, Senate Republicans will not stand idly by as the far-left, socialist wing of the Democrat Party attempts to unwind everything we’ve done,” he said. “Thankfully, we still have President Trump in the White House, and we’ll work with him to stop the worst impulses of Democrat extremism.”

Thune, 65, has served as the majority leader for nearly two years since winning a three-way race to succeed Mitch McConnell of Kentucky as the chamber’s top Republican. That was a spot McConnell had held since taking his party’s leadership reins in early 2007, making him the longest-serving Senate party leader in history, counting his time in both the minority and the majority.

Thune at times had a tumultuous relationship with the president as Trump pushed legislation, like the voter-ID related bill known as the SAVE America Act, that never had a chance of passing the chamber.

Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso of Wyoming is expected to seek his current role in the minority as well.

“Republicans had a tough night last night. We lost great Senators in hard races,” he said on X Wednesday afternoon. “There are clear lessons to be learned from the results.”

“We should listen to what voters unmistakably said last night,” Barrasso, 74, said. “In the Senate, we will aggressively oppose terrible ideas that drive our country toward the socialism Democrats embraced. Our commitment is to common sense. And our focus should not waiver from the top priority of driving down prices that have remained stubbornly too high.”

The leadership elections for Senate Republicans will take place on Tuesday, Nov. 10, at 9 a.m. in the Old Senate Chamber.

So far, no one has publicly come forward to challenge Thune, and his fellow Republican colleagues were already coalescing around him ahead of the midterms.

Florida Sen. Rick Scott, who ran against Thune in 2024 and is a friend of the president’s, said in September then he was not planning on challenging him again.

Sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., is expected to seek a repeat as vice chair of the Republican conference, while Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.V., is set to run again for Republican Policy Committee chair, according to people familiar with their plans.

#6051. GOP's midterm defeat sparks bold claims from foreign leaders who've clashed with Trump

Chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram joins 'The Faulkner Focus' to discuss the progressive agenda after Democrats sweep the midterms.

The GOP's sweeping midterm losses are drawing a positive response from several foreign leaders who have clashed with President Donald Trump, with some expressing hope that Democrats' victories could lead to a shift in U.S. policy on major global issues.

Democrats secured majorities in both the U.S. House of Representatives and the Senate in Tuesday's elections, setting the stage for a shift in congressional power in January and prompting reactions from officials in Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez took aim at Trump's policies in a Wednesday X post, suggesting that American voters had rejected the president's political agenda and predicting that a similar shift would soon take place in Spain.

"Yesterday, American society voted against policies that only make people poorer," Sánchez wrote. "Against hate. Against sexism. Against climate denial and against elite privilege."

AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI

A voter marks their ballot in the Kern County Elections Office on November 3, 2026 in Bakersfield, California. Americans go to the polls in consequential midterm elections, where control of the House and the Senate is at stake for the remainder of President Donald Trump's second term in office. (Mario Tama/Getty Images)

Sánchez has been an outspoken critic of U.S. and Israeli military operations against Iran, accusing Washington in March of "playing Russian roulette" with millions of lives. His opposition to the war and disputes with Trump over NATO defense spending have contributed to tensions between Madrid and Washington.

"We are not going to be complicit in something that is bad for the world and is also contrary to our values and interests, just out of fear of reprisals from someone," Sánchez said.

Prime Minister of Spain Pedro Sánchez Pérez-Castejón arrives at Huis ten Bosch Palace for a dinner hosted by the King and Queen of The Netherlands during the NATO Summit 2025 on June 24, 2025, in The Hague, Netherlands. (Patrick van Katwijk/Getty Images)

"Wild result in the USA last night! I'm cautiously optimistic on Europe's behalf," European Parliament Vice President Christel Schaldemose wrote in a Wednesday X post. "Not because everything now changes for the better, but because it could benefit the support for Ukraine, the green transition, and relations with the rest of the world."

Schaldemose criticized Trump’s interest in Greenland in January 2025, also suggesting that Europeans should "stand up for ourselves both in terms of the economy the global economy but also in terms of digital policy and the climate."

Britain's newly appointed Prime Minister Andy Burnham delivers a speech outside 10 Downing Street after taking office, in London, Britain, July 20, 2026. (REUTERS/Temilade Adelaja)

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Wednesday that the election results presented an opportunity for world leaders to work together to ease cost-of-living pressures and resolve the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, Sky News reported.

"Well, President Trump has accepted the results, and I feel the world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all - and that's the cost-of-living," Burnham said. "That has been the issue that I have put front and centre in my first three months in Downing Street, and we've made moves, but I can't get people's cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved."

Trump said in July that he had a "very good" conversation with Burnham about trade and security issues, although the two governments have since differed over Israeli settlement activity in the West Bank. In September, Britain announced plans to strengthen sanctions targeting settlements and prevent British companies from assisting settlement construction, drawing criticism from U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee.

Americans have been grappling with higher costs as the war in Iran has caused energy prices to surge. The U.S. affordability crisis was a major issue for voters heading into this year's midterms.

Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad ‌Baqer Ghalibaf claimed in a Wednesday social media post that U.S. voters "said NO TO WAR" amid cost-of-living concerns.

"Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message," Ghalibaf said, according to the Independent. "If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare."

Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara emphasized during a Wednesday press conference that the Japan-U.S. alliance "remains the cornerstone of Japan's foreign and security policy regardless of the outcome of the elections," Kyodo News reported.

Additionally, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa told reporters on Wednesday that he thinks the Democratic Party’s victory in the midterms will "introduce a new era in world relations," Reuters reported.

Trump confronted Ramaphosa during a May 2025 White House meeting, playing video footage that he claimed showed evidence of widespread violence against White South African farmers. Ramaphosa disputed Trump's allegations of persecution, while subsequent fact-checks found that some of the footage had been mischaracterized.

Trump claimed in a Tuesday night Truth Social post that if his name appeared on the ballot in the 2026 midterms the GOP would have "won IN A LANDSLIDE!"

Trump nevertheless congratulated Democrats on their victories and expressed a willingness to work with the incoming congressional majorities, while emphasizing that he would retain the power to veto legislation he opposes.

"They'll send over things that are insane, and I'll veto them," Trump told Fox News' Bret Baier on Tuesday night, adding that the two parties would eventually have to work together to get legislation passed.

#6050. Why Are Indonesians Dying in Ukraine?

Southeast Asia Brief: Why Are Indonesians Dying in Ukraine?

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Understanding the conflict four years in.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Southeast Asia Brief.

The highlights this week: Indonesia formally requests Russia to stop its war recruitment efforts there, an ASEAN envoy visits Myanmar, and Australia and China vie for influence in Timor-Leste.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Southeast Asia Brief.

The highlights this week: Indonesia formally requests Russia to stop its war recruitment efforts there, an ASEAN envoy visits Myanmar, and Australia and China vie for influence in Timor-Leste.

A Jakarta taxi driver in his 40s died in Ukraine after taking a contract to work for the Russian military, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence said last week. Taufiq Muhammad had undergone about a week and a half of training before being deployed and then killed in battle in May.

Then, on Sunday, Indonesia formally requested Russia to stop recruiting Indonesian citizens to serve as soldiers in its war in Ukraine.

Across Southeast Asia, men are—sometimes wittingly, sometimes not—being recruited into Russia’s war machine. Indonesia may be a hot spot. The death reported last week was just the latest in a series of incidents.

Last May, a former Indonesian Marine was confirmed to have joined the Russian military. His citizenship was revoked, and he is since rumored to have died. In January, a former member of Indonesia’s elite Brimob police unit was also confirmed to be fighting for Russia; he claimed for the Wagner Group. He also lost his citizenship. In September, a 30-year-old Indonesian man was reportedly killed in a drone strike in Ukraine.

In a press conference on Monday, the Indonesian National Police said cases involving 58 Indonesian citizens were currently being investigated by national and regional police authorities.

In September, Indonesia’s ambassador in Russia, Jose Tavares, told media that he had taken dozens of calls from families who thought their relatives had been recruited into the Russian military.

In an interview with Foreign Policy, Radityo Dharmaputra, an Indonesian academic who has researched this topic, called the Indonesian government’s response this week “a necessary step, albeit ineffective.”

Radityo said Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto should now appeal personally to Russian President Vladimir Putin, whom he has met on numerous occasions, to stop the recruiting.

Indonesia should also put pressure on Russia publicly, Radityo added. Other actions he recommended included canceling cooperation if Moscow doesn’t halt its recruiting efforts, stopping migrant workers going to Russia, and generally discouraging travel there. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) could also establish a framework to deal with the problem, Radityo suggested.

Indeed, it is not just Indonesians who are getting pulled into Russia’s war machine. Data released by Ukraine and published by StopRussianRecruiters.org lists 44 Southeast Asians who had surrendered themselves to become prisoners of war. Of those listed, 16 are Vietnamese, 14 are Filipino, 10 are Indonesian, two are Cambodian, one is from Myanmar, and one is Malaysian.

There are also reports that three Filipinos and a Vietnamese man were killed fighting in Ukraine for Russia.

Munira Mustaffa, the executive director of Chasseur Group and a senior fellow at Verve Research, has compared Russian recruitment tactics on social media to those used by criminals in scam centers.

Some of the Southeast Asians on the front lines, like the Marine and the former police officer, seem to know what they were volunteering for. Many others were recruited by deceptive jobs ads and then pressed into the Russian military and thrown onto the battlefield with minimal training.

“Many men were enticed to Russia with promises of blue-collar work, not expecting to serve on the front line,” Munira said in an interview with me.

Munira has said Southeast Asian recruits are just a “small fraction” compared with those from South Asia, Central Asia, and Africa. She suggested that Russia is perhaps reluctant to upset ASEAN countries, with which it has stepped up diplomatic ties following its invasion of Ukraine.

However, an investigation by the German TV news program Tagesschau in July found evidence that Russia is now targeting Cambodia, Indonesia, and Malaysia for recruitment. Backlash elsewhere, including Kenya, had pushed Russia to change where it recruited.

The regional response has been muted. Outside of Indonesia, the only notable response has been from the Philippines, which in October announced an investigation into illegal recruitment activities.

Munira also called for an ASEAN-level response drawing on its experience dealing with human trafficking and scam centers.

“The deceptive and predatory practices involved, including war profiteering, could be replicated in other conflicts, both within and beyond this region, because they offer a template for exploiting migrant labor.”

ASEAN visits Myanmar. Last Thursday, Philippine Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro, the ASEAN envoy on Myanmar, met Myanmar junta Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe in the capital of Naypyitaw as part of a two-day trip.

Myanmar state media reported that the two discussed normalizing Myanmar’s status in ASEAN, which has excluded junta leaders from summits since the country’s 2021 coup. Lazaro’s own statements made no mention of this.

There is no indication that Lazaro met with Aung San Suu Kyi, the leader of Myanmar’s democratic opposition who has been detained since 2021—though Lazaro told Philippine media that the junta had said she was “doing well.”

Meanwhile, on Friday, Reuters broke the story that Japan was pushing for the Financial ​Action Task Force, a global financial crimes watchdog, to remove Myanmar from its blacklist.

As we’ve previously covered, Myanmar’s junta is making serious progress in its quest for diplomatic legitimacy.

On Saturday, shortly after Lazaro’s trip ended, the junta bombed an area held by Karen rebels on the Thai border, damaging homes and public buildings in Thailand. Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said on Monday that the Thai military had conveyed its concerns to Myanmar. He added: “The fighting has nothing to do with Thailand or Thai people.”

Vietnam overtakes Indonesia. Vietnam is set to become richer than Indonesia on a GDP per capita basis, according to International Monetary Fund (IMF) data released in October. The first outlet to spot this seems to have been Nikkei Asia.

According to IMF projections, Vietnam’s nominal per capita GDP will hit $5,259 this year—an annual rise of 8.9 percent and nearly double what it was a decade ago. (Indonesia’s is projected at $5,153.)

Vietnam’s breakneck growth, 9.95 percent in the last quarter alone, means it is rapidly making ground on other economies in the region. Current IMF projections suggest that it will have an economy larger than Thailand’s by 2028, though it only aims to hit Thailand’s current per capita income by 2030.

Driving this boom are strong exports and infrastructure investment, which means projected growth was revised up despite the fuel shock. A U.S. trade investigation that could result in new tariffs poses a potential challenge, however.

Another question is, is this being felt by ordinary Vietnamese? As I noted last week, despite the rapid growth, young Vietnamese, like other young Southeast Asians, are struggling to secure jobs.

Bangsamoro choses leader. A month and a half after the first-ever elections for the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in the Philippines’s Mindanao archipelago were held—and delivered a hung parliament—the Bangsamoro Parliament chose its first chief minister, Abdulraof Macacua of the Bangsamoro Federalist Party, on Friday.

Macacua is a former chief of staff of the armed wing of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF), which signed the peace deal that led to these elections. But he broke with the leadership and formed his own party, won 31 seats, and has now secured a parliamentary majority with the support of various other parties.

Losing out is Ahod “Al-Haj Murad” Ebrahim, the chairman of the MILF and leader of the United Bangsamoro Justice Party, which won 30 seats.

Happily, Murad seems to have accepted the result. With thousands of MILF fighters still yet to be demobilized, there was a real potential for danger if he felt cheated.

In his victory speech, Macacua addressed Murad in a conciliatory way, declaring that he recognized the “sacrifices, principles, and aspirations upon which this vision was built” and considered it “both a personal commitment and a moral responsibility to carry it forward, no matter what.”

The next challenge will the demobilization of MILF fighters.

3,560. The number of deaths caused by smoke from Indonesia’s forest fires in September, according to estimates by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air. Indonesia is facing its worst forest fires in a decade, which continued to rage through October. However, last week saw intermittent rain in some hot spots, raising hopes that the delayed wet season had finally arrived.

Cambodian women who worked in the scam industry are turning to sex work as the crackdown drives the industry abroad, according to an interesting article in Cambodia: Rain and Dust.

In the South China Morning Post, Vincent Tan spots signs of a housing bubble in key Southeast Asian markets.

Two Supreme Court rulings in the Philippines could shake up its politics and make corruption trickier, Mong Palatino writes in the Diplomat.

A security pact and a gas deal have put new focus on the tussle between Australia and China for influence in Timor-Leste.

In recent years, Australia has been moving to rapidly upgrade its relationships with Pacific islands to counter growing Chinese influence in the region. This has taken the form of alliances and security pacts, some of which explicitly block Chinese bases from being built in these nations.

Timor, Australian Defense Minister Richard Marles has declared, is the “last link in the chain.”

In August, Chinese Defense Minister Dong Jun visited Timor and said China was “willing to work with Timor-Leste to take military-to-military relations to a new level.”

Australia’s response came when it and Timor signed a security agreement in October worth $43.5 million, with Canberra providing patrol vessels as well as help upgrading Timor’s cybersecurity and disaster response capacity. The move was widely seen as aimed at countering Chinese influence.

Still, this is well short of the strong arrangements that Australia has struck elsewhere.

China has also built economic presence and goodwill. By some estimates, 20,000 Chinese citizens since 2002 may have moved to Timor, where they now play a key role in the restaurant and retail sector.

The surprise decision last Tuesday by Australian company Woodside Energy to sell its stake in the Greater Sunrise gas field that Australia shared with Timor has no doubt prompted further anxiety in Canberra. Timor had previously threatened to turn to Chinese developers when Woodside demurred at government demands for a refinery in Timor.

It’s unclear if this threat is credible. And after Woodside’s exit, Timor’s advisors said Japanese and Middle Eastern companies—not Chinese ones—had expressed interest in stepping in. But that hasn’t stopped Australian media from worrying.

Joseph Rachman is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Southeast Asia Brief. He is a freelance journalist based in Bangkok. X: @rachman_joseph
